issues.failure_explanation: By the general formula K_\infty(y_0)=1/|\widehat{w}^{(1,1,2)}\widehat{y}_0| with \widehat{w}^{(1,1,2)}=[1 1 1], the condition number is K_\infty(y_0)=\Vert y_0\Vert_1/|y_{01}+y_{02}+y_{03}|. The displayed chain asserts the false equality \Vert y_0\Vert_1=|y_{01}|+|y_{02}|+|y_{03}|, which equals the 1-norm only when the components of y_0 have equal signs (e.g. y_0=(1,2,3) but not y_0=(-1,1,0.05) or (-0.8,-2.9,1.4), two of the three cases shown). The two sides differ whenever sign(y_{0\ell}) are not all equal, and the claimed equality of the two displayed expressions is not a theorem.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
For $y_0$ and $\widehat{z}_0$ satisfying the RLGE condition, we have
$$ 
K(t,y_0,\widehat{z}_0)\sim K_\infty(t,y_0,\widehat{z}_0):= \frac{\left\Vert
	Q_1(t)\widehat{z}_{0}\right\Vert }{\left\Vert Q_1(t)\widehat{y}
	_{0}\right\Vert },\ t\rightarrow +\infty,
Note that if $u$ does not satisfy the RLGE condition, then $Q_1(t)u = 0$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

issues.failure_explanation: Properties (\ref{infQ1}) and (\ref{infQ1u}) are asserted without any proof or reference and are used crucially: point 2 after Theorem \ref{Theorem4} and fact B) (boundedness and uniform non-vanishing of the asymptotic relative error) rest on them. They are nontrivial: Q_1(t) is a finite sum of trigonometric oscillating rank-one terms, and the claims (\ref{infQ1u}) and its matrix analogue are exactly the statement that this finite trigonometric sum never approaches the zero operator / zero vector, which is a genuine nontrivial fact (it fails for a single term e^{i\omega t}vu^T whose scalar coefficient oscillates through zero, and holds only because for RLGE-u the vector-valued sum stays outside every neighbourhood of 0 uniformly in t; the matrix statement additionally requires a uniform lower bound over all t of the norm of a sum of terms with potentially cancelling phases). The paper cites \cite{Maset2022} for proofs of Theorem \ref{Theorem4} but presents (\ref{infQ1})-(\ref{infQ1u}) as standalone claims in the body, and the surrounding quantitative Section 5 bounds (Theorem \ref{onset}) provide no estimate that would yield a uniform-in-t lower bound. As written, the two claimed uniform bounds are unsupported nontrivial assertions on which fact B) depends.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: At minimum, supply the (finite-dimensional trigonometric) argument that a finite sum \sum e^{i\omega_i t}\alpha_i v_i with linearly independent v_i and not-all-zero coefficients is bounded below uniformly in t, and that the same holds for the operator sum with linearly independent rank-one summands; this is a contained standard compactness/trigonometric-polynomial argument.
issues.overall_effect: The central boundedness/uniform-nonvanishing claims about K_\infty (point 2 after Theorem \ref{Theorem4}) and qualitative fact B) rely on an unproved uniform lower bound; if it failed, the advertised guarantee that the asymptotic relative error is bounded away from zero uniformly in t would be unsupported.
issues.title: Unjustified uniform-in-t lower bound on ||Q_1(t)u|| behind Theorem 4
issues.why_classification: The missing argument is a genuine nontrivial step (uniform lower bound for a trigonometric polynomial vector/operator), but it is a contained standard result whose addition preserves all stated conclusions and rates unchanged.

issues.failure_explanation: Two independent checks show the displayed chain cannot be correct as an equality. (i) Dimensional/consistency check: with \widehat{z}_0=(0,\pm1)/\Vert(0,1)\Vert= (0,\pm1), the numerator |\widehat{w}^{(1)}\widehat{z}_0| must equal |w^{(1)}_2|/\Vert w^{(1)}\Vert=1/\Vert w^{(1)}\Vert, which is dimensionless and, for the instance (\ref{instanceGDPND}) where the left eigenvector is proportional to (1,-1) in the Euclidean norm, equals 1/\sqrt 2 \approx 0.7071. But the closed form sqrt{1+B(0)^2} = sqrt{1+0.61^2} = 1.1694 is not 0.7071, so the two sides disagree; substituting B(0)=0.61 into the displayed expression gives 1.1694/0.39 = 2.9985, while the stated value is 3.0035 (and the limiting relative error 0.025641 = 3.0035 \times 0.0082645 uses the latter). The numerical discrepancy shows at least one of the displayed closed form, the numeric value, or the asserted identity is wrong; the discrepancy is not a single forced typo, and the surrounding reasoning (which value the relative error tends to) depends on which piece is corrected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Recompute and restate the closed form of K_\infty(y_0,\widehat{z}_0) from the left eigenvector of the instance (\ref{instanceGDPND}) so that it is consistent with the numerator |\widehat{w}^{(1)}\widehat{z}_0| = |w^{(1)}_2|/\Vert w^{(1)}\Vert, and correct the numeric value 3.0035 (and the limit 0.025641) accordingly; this requires recomputing the eigenvector normalization and the limit in Figure \ref{Figura55}.
issues.overall_effect: The example's headline asymptotic value for the directional condition number (and hence the claimed limiting relative error 0.025641 and the illustrative contrast with the singular case B(0)=1) is not reliably supported by the displayed formula.
issues.title: Expression for K_\infty(y_0,z_0) in the GDP-ND example inconsistent with its closed form and numeric value
issues.why_classification: Repairing the chain requires recomputing an eigenvector normalization and one numeric constant, and possibly re-deriving which of the displayed equalities is at fault; contained, but not a single forced correction, and one substantive displayed claim must be withdrawn or corrected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
For $y_0$ and $\widehat{z}_0$ satisfying the RLGE condition, we have
$$ 
K(t,y_0,\widehat{z}_0)\sim K_\infty(t,y_0,\widehat{z}_0):= \frac{\left\Vert
	Q_1(t)\widehat{z}_{0}\right\Vert }{\left\Vert Q_1(t)\widehat{y}
	_{0}\right\Vert },\ t\rightarrow +\infty,
K_\infty\left( t,y_{0},\widehat{z}_{0}\right) = \mathrm{OSF}(y_0,\widehat{z}_0)\cdot\mathrm{OT}(t,y_0,\widehat{z}_0)

issues.failure_explanation: Fact B) says the relative error 'converges to... an oscillating function' when the rightmost eigenvalue is non-real. But K_\infty(t,y_0,\widehat{z}_0)=OSF\cdot OT(t,\cdot) is a periodic (not convergent) function of t in that case: OT has period \pi/\omega_1 and is genuinely oscillating (this is the paper's own terminology and content of Theorem \ref{Thcomplex}); the relative error \delta(t)=K(t,y_0,\widehat{z}_0)\varepsilon likewise does not converge but oscillates asymptotically. The prose phrase 'it converges to... an oscillating function' is thus self-contradictory as a mathematical claim about \lim_{t\to\infty}\delta(t): no convergence takes place; only the ratio to K_\infty tends to 1. Fact B) is a summary promise about the relative error and, as worded, asserts a limit that does not exist in the complex-eigenvalue case.

failure_location.quote: \item [B)] \emph{In a generic situation for the initial value and the perturbation of the initial value (namely they satisfy the RLGE condition), the relative error of the perturbed solution asymptotically (as $t\rightarrow +\infty$) neither diverges nor decays to zero. Instead, it converges to a non-zero constant, in case of a real eigenvalue as  rightmost eigenvalue, and to an oscillating function bounded and uniformly away from zero, otherwise.}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reword fact B) to say that in the complex case the relative error is asymptotically equal to (relative error tending to 0 against) a bounded, uniformly non-vanishing periodic function, mirroring the precise Theorem \ref{Theorem4}/Thcomplex statements.
issues.overall_effect: The headline qualitative summary of the paper's main asymptotic result, presented to readers as the analogue of fact A), misdescribes the complex-eigenvalue case by asserting convergence where only asymptotic periodic oscillation (ratio tending to 1) holds.
issues.title: Bold conclusion B) overstates Theorem 4: 'converges to a non-zero constant' not established for non-real rightmost eigenvalues
issues.why_classification: A local wording repair of a summary sentence restores full consistency with the theorems; no rate, regime, or dependent result is lost.
